transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hey Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. Uh, well, what brought me in is... basically, people keep getting on my case, saying I’m not listening to them. 

Like my supervisor at the plant, or my wife. They'll be talking straight to me, right? Just looking right at me. And... well, speaking of my supervisor, he was just on my back yesterday about the new stamping press. We got this new machine on the production floor and it's supposed to be faster, but it keeps jamming on the quarter-inch plates. I told him the alignment was off, but he wouldn't hear it. The maintenance guy, Frank, he's a good guy, but he's been out sick with some kind of flu, so the whole line is just a mess right now. 

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, listening. Yeah, so my supervisor or my wife will be talking right to my face, and a minute later I realize I only caught maybe half of what they said. So I have to ask them to say it all over again, and man, they get so mad. Especially my wife, like if she's talking about her sister's new dog or something. Have you ever had a Golden Retriever? They shed like crazy, it gets all over the couch. But yeah, that's why I'm here, I guess. The listening thing.
Have you always struggled with this kind of focus, or is this something that has only started happening more recently?

Always? Yeah, definitely always. Even back when I was a kid, like way before middle school, I was exactly like this. My teachers were constantly moving my seat because I just couldn't stay put. I'd be up and down, calling out the answers without raising my hand, always getting in trouble for butting into what the other kids were working on. 

I remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable. She had this huge wooden desk up front. They really don't make furniture like that anymore, you know? Solid oak. My uncle actually does woodworking on the side, makes these beautiful coffee tables and cabinets. He tried to teach me how to do it once, but you gotta wait so long for the wood glue to dry and the varnish to set, and I just can't stand sitting around waiting for paint to dry, literally. I'd rather be doing something with my hands that moves fast, which is why I like the production line, usually, when the machines actually work. 

But anyway, yeah, Mrs. Gable moved my desk right next to hers, right up against the chalkboard. The chalk dust used to get all over my clothes. My mom hated that. She was always scrubbing at my jeans. Speaking of which, the new uniforms at the plant pick up grease like you wouldn't believe. I don't know what kind of fabric they switched to, but it's terrible.
